A1:
Syllabus: Accounting Standards in India, Ind AS, IFRS, US GAAP, GAAP vs IFRS, transfer pricing. Asked: 4–6 questions every session (highest in Module A). Old papers asked "AS 18 relates to…". The May 2026 paper instead gave a business situation and asked which treatment the standard requires (AS 3, 4, 7, 10, 12, 18, 22, 26, Ind AS 116). Learn each standard as a rule + its exceptions.

1. Who makes the standards

  • ICAI's Accounting Standards Board (ASB) formulates standards. The Central Government notifies them under the Companies Act 2013 (Sec 133) after advice from NFRA (National Financial Reporting Authority, which replaced NACAS).
  • Two sets exist side by side:
    • AS (Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules 2021) for companies not on Ind AS.
    • Ind AS (Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules 2015) converged with IFRS.
  • Ind AS road map:
    • Phase I: FY 2016-17, listed or unlisted companies with net worth ≥ ₹500 crore.
    • Phase II: FY 2017-18, all listed companies, and unlisted companies with net worth ≥ ₹250 crore.
    • Holding, subsidiary, JV and associate companies of these follow too.
    • NBFCs: net worth ≥ ₹500 crore from 2018-19; others ≥ ₹250 crore from 2019-20.
    • Banks: RBI has deferred Ind AS for scheduled commercial banks until further notice, so banks still follow AS plus RBI norms.
  • Once a company follows Ind AS it cannot switch back to AS.
  • IFRS are issued by the IASB, London. US GAAP is issued by FASB.

2. IFRS vs US GAAP (asked as statements)

PointIFRS / Ind ASUS GAAP
ApproachPrinciples-basedRules-based (detailed guidance)
LIFO for inventoryProhibitedPermitted
Revaluation of PPEAllowed (revaluation model)Not allowed (cost only)
Development costCapitalised if criteria metGenerally expensed
Reversal of impairmentAllowed (not for goodwill)Not allowed
Extraordinary itemsProhibitedAlso eliminated (since 2015)
Indian AS 2 also prohibits LIFO. The allowed cost formulas are FIFO, weighted average, and specific identification (for items not ordinarily interchangeable).

3. The standards — number, name, and the rule examiners test

ASSubjectThe point that gets tested
1Disclosure of Accounting PoliciesFundamental assumptions: going concern, consistency, accrual. If followed, no disclosure is needed. If not followed, disclose. Policy selection: prudence, substance over form, materiality.
2Valuation of InventoriesLower of cost and NRV, item by item.
  • Cost excludes: abnormal waste, storage (unless needed in production), admin overheads, selling costs.
  • Not covered by AS 2: WIP under construction contracts (AS 7), financial instruments, livestock/agri/forest produce and mineral ores held at NRV by trade practice.
3Cash Flow StatementsOperating / Investing / Financing classification. See chapter B4.
4Events after the Balance Sheet DateAdjusting events give evidence of conditions that existed at BS date → adjust. Non-adjusting events → disclose only. A proposed dividend declared after BS date is not a liability, only disclosed. If going concern fails after BS date, the whole basis changes.
5Net Profit, Prior Period Items, Change in PoliciesPrior period items (errors/omissions of earlier years found now) → shown separately in current P&L. Change in estimate (useful life, residual value) → prospective. Change in policy only if required by statute or AS, or for better presentation.
7Construction ContractsPercentage of completion when outcome is reliable. Expected loss is recognised immediately. If the outcome is not reliable, recognise revenue only up to recoverable cost.
9Revenue RecognitionGoods: when significant risks and rewards are transferred and there is no significant uncertainty. Interest: time basis. Royalty: accrual. Dividend: when the right to receive is established.
10Property, Plant & EquipmentCost and capitalisation rules, component approach, major inspection. See chapter A7. (AS 6 Depreciation was merged into AS 10.)
11Changes in Foreign Exchange RatesMonetary items at closing rate. Exchange difference goes to P&L. Non-monetary items at historical rate.
12Government GrantsSee section 4.
13InvestmentsCurrent: lower of cost and fair value. Long-term: cost less permanent decline.
14AmalgamationsPooling of interests (merger) vs purchase method.
15Employee BenefitsShort-term, post-employment (defined contribution vs defined benefit), termination benefits.
16Borrowing CostsCapitalise for a qualifying asset (one that takes a substantial period, normally 12 months or more, to get ready). Suspend capitalisation during extended interruption. Stop when the asset is substantially ready.
17Segment ReportingBusiness and geographical segments; 10% thresholds.
18Related Party DisclosuresSee section 5.
19LeasesFinance vs operating lease by substance (risks and rewards). Does not cover land leases or natural-resource leases. Ind AS 116 replaced the distinction for lessees. See chapter C8.
20Earnings Per ShareBasic and diluted EPS. A bonus issue is adjusted retrospectively. See chapter B3.
21Consolidated Financial StatementsParent + subsidiaries.
22Taxes on IncomeDeferred tax on timing differences only, not permanent ones. See chapter B3.
23 / 27Associates in CFS / Joint VenturesEquity method / proportionate consolidation.
24Discontinuing OperationsDisclosure from the initial disclosure event.
25Interim Financial ReportingEach interim period is part of the annual period.
26Intangible AssetsSee section 6.
28Impairment of AssetsImpairment loss = carrying amount − recoverable amount, where recoverable amount is the higher of net selling price and value in use.
29Provisions, Contingent Liabilities & AssetsProvision: present obligation from a past event + probable outflow + reliable estimate. Contingent liability: disclose. Contingent asset: neither recognised nor disclosed in the financial statements.

Withdrawn numbers: AS 6 (merged into AS 10), AS 8 (into AS 26), AS 30–32. A question like "AS 6 deals with…" is a trap.

4. AS 12 Government Grants — the four cases

Grant typeTreatment
Related to a specific depreciable assetEither deduct from the asset's cost (depreciation is then on the net amount), or treat as deferred income and release to P&L over useful life in proportion to depreciation.
Related to a non-depreciable asset (e.g. land), no obligationCredit to capital reserve. If conditions require obligations, release to income over the period of those costs.
Promoters' contribution type (e.g. based on total investment, no repayment)Capital reserve, as part of shareholders' funds.
Revenue grant (to meet costs)P&L, either as income or deducted from the related expense, matched with the cost.
  • Recognise a grant only when there is reasonable assurance that the conditions will be met and the grant will be received. Receiving cash alone is not the test.
  • Refund of a grant is shown as an extraordinary item.
  • Grant in the form of a non-monetary asset given free: record at nominal value. If given at concessional rate: at acquisition cost.

5. AS 18 Related Parties

  • Related means one party can control or exercise significant influence over the other. Significant influence is participation in financial and operating policy, not control. Shareholding of 20% or more is presumed significant influence.
  • Covered:
    • holding, subsidiary and fellow-subsidiary companies
    • associates and joint ventures
    • individuals with voting power giving control or significant influence, and their relatives
    • Key Management Personnel (KMP) and their relatives
    • enterprises over which any of these have significant influence (e.g. a firm in which a director is a partner)
  • NOT related merely because of:
    • two companies having a common director
    • providers of finance, trade unions, public utilities, government departments in normal dealings
    • a single customer, supplier or agent with whom there is a large volume of business
  • Disclose even if no price is charged (e.g. an interest-free loan to the MD). The test is the relationship, not cash or profit.
  • Exemptions:
    • intra-group transactions eliminated in consolidated statements
    • a state-controlled enterprise's transactions with other state-controlled enterprises
    • where disclosure would conflict with a duty of confidentiality (e.g. a bank's duty to customers)

6. AS 26 Intangible Assets

  • Intangible asset: identifiable, non-monetary, without physical substance, controlled, and expected to give future benefits.
  • Research phase → always expense.
  • Development phase → capitalise only if all six are shown:
    1. technical feasibility
    2. intention to complete
    3. ability to use or sell
    4. how it will generate future benefits (a market exists)
    5. adequate resources
    6. cost can be measured reliably
  • If research and development can't be separated, treat everything as research.
  • Never recognised as an asset: internally generated goodwill, brands, mastheads, publishing titles and customer lists.
  • Always expensed: start-up costs, training, advertising and promotion, relocation.
  • Patent registration fees directly attributable to an asset are capitalised.
  • Amortisation: rebuttable presumption that useful life is not more than 10 years from the date the asset is available for use. Residual value is presumed nil.

7. Transfer pricing

  • Price charged between associated enterprises (e.g. an Indian subsidiary buying from its foreign parent).
  • Tax law requires the Arm's Length Price (ALP): the price unrelated parties would charge. Without this rule, groups would shift profit to low-tax countries by over- or under-pricing.
  • Income-tax Act 1961, Sections 92–92F. Covers international transactions and specified domestic transactions.
  • Methods (Rule 10B):
    • Comparable Uncontrolled Price (CUP)
    • Resale Price Method
    • Cost Plus Method
    • Profit Split Method
    • Transactional Net Margin Method (TNMM)
    • any other method
  • An accountant's report is required in Form 3CEB.
  • Transfer pricing cannot be set freely by "group policy". The Transfer Pricing Officer can adjust income up to ALP.
Traps:
  • "Cash received, so take the grant to income": wrong. Grants follow AS 12 matching, not receipt.
  • Change in useful life or residual value = change in estimate → prospective (AS 5). It is not a prior-period item and is not restated.
  • A customer becoming insolvent after the BS date, from difficulties that existed before → adjusting. A fire after the BS date → non-adjusting (disclose if material).
  • AS 7: recognise a foreseeable loss on the whole contract at once, even if work is only 10% done.
  • AS 26: advertising before launch is never an intangible. Development after feasibility can be.
  • Common director alone ≠ related party. A firm in which a director is a partner = related party.
  • Contingent asset is not disclosed in the financial statements. Contingent liability is disclosed unless the outflow is remote.
A2:
Syllabus: Basic accountancy procedures (concepts, going concern, double entry, conservatism, revenue recognition, accrual vs cash) + Balance Sheet Equation (Module B). Asked: 3–4 questions on concepts plus 1–3 on the equation every session. May 2026: "which concept contradicts this view", "match the concept with its use", "profit always increases liabilities?", "cash basis vs accrual".

1. Concepts (assumptions) vs conventions

ConceptMeaningWhere it shows up in questions
Business entityBusiness is separate from the owner, even in a sole proprietorship (where it is not legally separate).Owner's personal insurance paid from business = drawings. Capital is a liability of the business to the owner. Profit added to capital.
Money measurementOnly events measurable in money are recorded.Staff morale, a CEO's skill and a strike threat are not recorded.
Going concernBusiness will continue for the foreseeable future.Basis for showing assets at cost less depreciation (not liquidation value), prepaid expenses as assets, and classifying current and non-current items.
Accounting periodLife is split into periods (FY April–March).Basis for accruals and adjustments.
Cost (historical cost)Assets are recorded at acquisition cost, not market value.Car bought for ₹10 lakh, now worth ₹12 lakh → still ₹10 lakh.
Dual aspectEvery transaction has two equal effects: Assets = Liabilities + Capital.Basis of double entry.
Realisation / revenue recognitionRevenue is recognised when earned (goods transferred, service rendered), not when cash is received.Goods on approval are not revenue until approved.
AccrualRecord income when earned and expense when incurred, regardless of cash. It distinguishes the right to receive cash from the receipt of cash.Outstanding and prepaid expenses, accrued income.
MatchingExpenses of a period are matched with that period's revenue.Depreciation, closing stock, unexpired insurance.
Objectivity / verifiabilityEntries are supported by vouchers and evidence.—
ConventionMeaning
Conservatism (prudence)"Anticipate no profit, provide for all possible losses." Examples: stock at lower of cost or NRV; provision for doubtful debts; no provision for discount on creditors. It is applied with care: no secret reserves.
ConsistencySame methods year to year for comparability. Change only for valid reasons (AS 5).
MaterialityInsignificant items need not be shown separately (e.g. a stapler bought is expensed even if it lasts years).
Full disclosureAll material information is disclosed (notes, contingent liabilities).

AS 1 names three fundamental accounting assumptions: going concern, consistency and accrual. If they are followed, no disclosure is needed; if not followed, disclose.

2. Cash basis vs accrual basis

  • Cash basis records only receipts and payments. It ignores outstanding fees, prepaid rent and unpaid bills, so profit is distorted.
  • The Companies Act (Sec 128) requires accrual basis and double entry for companies.
  • Some professionals and small entities may use the cash basis, so it is not prohibited for every entity.

3. Stages of accounting

Recording (journal, subsidiary books) → Classifying (ledger) → Summarising (trial balance, final accounts) → Analysing and interpreting → Communicating (reporting).

  • Concepts like dual aspect, money measurement and objectivity work at the recording stage.
  • Going concern, consistency, conservatism, materiality and full disclosure are reporting-stage concepts.
  • Accounting is called the language of business.
  • Book-keeping is the recording part only; accounting is wider.
  • Limitations of accounting: it ignores non-monetary facts, is based on historical cost (price changes ignored), and relies on estimates (depreciation, provisions).

4. Balance Sheet (accounting) equation

Assets = Liabilities + Capital
Capital = Assets − Liabilities.
Closing capital = Opening capital + Fresh capital + Profit − Drawings (profit raises capital; loss and drawings reduce it).
TransactionAssetsLiabilitiesCapital
Owner introduces cash↑—↑
Buy furniture for cash↑↓ (no change in total)——
Buy goods on credit↑↑—
Pay a creditor / repay a loan↓↓—
Pay salary (expense)↓—↓
Expense outstanding—↑↓
Owner withdraws cash↓—↓
Sale of goods (cost 60) for 100 cash↑40 net—↑40
Convert a creditor's dues into a loan—one ↑ one ↓—
Equity converted into a loan—↑↓
Dividend declared (not yet paid)—↑↓

Profit and liabilities: profit first increases capital (owners' equity) through retained earnings. It touches liabilities only when management later declares a dividend (liability ↑) or uses the cash to repay debt (liability ↓). So "profit always increases liabilities" is wrong.

Worked example: Cash ₹40,000, debtors ₹60,000, stock ₹50,000, machinery ₹1,50,000, creditors ₹70,000, bank loan ₹1,00,000. Assets = 3,00,000; liabilities = 1,70,000; capital = ₹1,30,000.

Traps:
  • Capital is a liability of the business (business entity concept), even though it belongs to the owner.
  • Asset bought for ₹10 lakh, market value ₹12 lakh → record at ₹10 lakh (cost concept, not conservatism).
  • "Anticipate no profit, provide for all losses" = conservatism. "Same method every year" = consistency.
  • Prepaid expense being an asset rests on accrual plus going concern.
  • Purchase of an asset for cash does not change total assets.
A3:
Syllabus: Maintenance of cash/subsidiary books and ledger, record keeping, account categories, debit and credit, journalising. Asked: 1–5 questions on golden rules/journal plus 1–2 on types of accounts per session. May 2026 asked "Machinery is a real account so debit it every time?", classification of Goodwill and Outstanding Salary, petty cash under the imprest system, and journal entries for credit purchase and capital brought in.

1. Traditional (British) classification and golden rules

TypeExamplesRule
Personal
  • Natural: persons
  • Artificial: firms, companies, banks, clubs
  • Representative: accounts standing for a person
Ram, ABC Ltd, Bank, Capital, Drawings, Loan from bank. Representative: Outstanding salary, Prepaid rent, Accrued interest, Income received in advance.Debit the receiver, credit the giver
Real
  • Tangible
  • Intangible
Cash, stock, machinery, building, furniture. Intangible: Goodwill, patents, trademarks.Debit what comes in, credit what goes out
NominalExpenses, losses, incomes, gains: salary, rent, discount allowed/received, depreciation, interest, commission, bad debts.Debit all expenses and losses, credit all incomes and gains

2. Modern (accounting-equation) classification

AccountIncreaseDecreaseNormal balance
AssetsDebitCreditDebit
Expenses / lossesDebitCreditDebit
LiabilitiesCreditDebitCredit
CapitalCreditDebitCredit
Revenue / gainsCreditDebitCredit

Memory line for a trial balance: assets and expenses have debit balances; liabilities, capital and income have credit balances. Drawings has a debit balance (it reduces capital).

3. "It's a real account, so always debit it?" — capital vs revenue first

  • Golden rules tell you which side; capital-vs-revenue tells you which account.
  • Spending that brings or enhances future economic benefit (purchase price, installation, freight to bring a machine, major component replacement) → debit Machinery.
  • Routine repairs, lubricants and servicing → debit Repairs / Maintenance (nominal), even though they relate to machinery.
  • Insurance claim received for damage to machinery: Dr Bank, Cr Insurance claim / Loss by damage. It is not a debit to Machinery.

4. Typical entries examiners twist

TransactionEntry
Goods bought on credit from AA LtdPurchases A/c Dr; To AA Ltd
Furniture bought on creditFurniture A/c Dr; To Supplier (not Purchases — Purchases is only for goods traded)
Owner brings additional cashCash/Bank Dr; To Capital
Goods withdrawn by ownerDrawings Dr; To Purchases (at cost)
Goods given as free samples / charityAdvertisement / Charity Dr; To Purchases
Goods lost by fire (insured, claim partly admitted)Insurance claim Dr + Loss by fire Dr; To Purchases
Cash received from debtor after discountCash Dr + Discount allowed Dr; To Debtor
Paid outstanding electricityOutstanding electricity Dr; To Bank
Machinery bought by issuing sharesMachinery Dr; To Vendor; then Vendor Dr; To Share Capital
Rent for April paid on 28 MarchPrepaid rent Dr; To Cash
Bad debt written offBad debts Dr; To Debtor
Bad debt recovered laterCash Dr; To Bad debts recovered (income), not to the debtor
Interest on capital allowedInterest on capital Dr; To Capital
DepreciationDepreciation Dr; To Asset (or Provision for depreciation)

5. Books of original entry (subsidiary books)

BookWhat goes in
Cash book (single/double/triple column)All cash and bank receipts and payments. It is both a book of original entry and a ledger. Triple column: cash, bank, discount. The discount columns are memorandum only and are totalled and posted.
Purchases bookOnly credit purchases of goods (not assets, not cash purchases)
Sales bookOnly credit sales of goods
Purchase returns (returns outward) bookGoods returned to suppliers; supported by a debit note
Sales returns (returns inward) bookGoods returned by customers; supported by a credit note
Bills receivable / payable booksBills received / accepted
Journal properOpening and closing entries, adjustments, rectification, credit purchase of assets, and anything that fits no other book

Petty cash, imprest system:

  • The cashier gives the petty cashier a fixed float (the imprest).
  • At the end of the period the petty cashier is reimbursed exactly what was spent, so the float is restored.
  • Entry on giving or reimbursing: Petty Cash A/c Dr; To Cash/Bank.
  • Expenses are later posted from the analytical petty cash book: individual expense accounts Dr; To Petty Cash.

Contra entry: a transaction affecting both the cash and bank columns, e.g. cash deposited into bank or cash withdrawn. Mark it "C".

Ledger: the book of final entry. Posting from the journal is followed by balancing. The trial balance is prepared from ledger balances.

Traps:
  • Outstanding salary, prepaid rent and accrued interest are representative personal accounts, not nominal.
  • Goodwill is an intangible real account.
  • Capital and drawings are personal accounts (of the proprietor).
  • Discount allowed and discount received are nominal accounts. Trade discount is never recorded.
  • Credit purchase of furniture goes to the journal proper, not the purchases book.
  • A sales return wrongly entered as a purchase is an error of principle/commission. To fix it: Sales Return Dr; To Purchases.
A4:
Syllabus: Trial balance (meaning, features, types, disagreement), classification and location of errors, rectification, suspense account, rectification after books are closed, adjusting and closing entries. Asked: 2–5 questions every session, always among the top Module A topics. May 2026 gave 5 case questions: machine entered in the purchases book (effect on fixed assets, profit and TB), a full sale omitted, errors of principle, suspense corrections and profit, and "which errors affect TB".

1. Trial balance (TB)

  • A statement (not an account) of ledger balances on a date, to check arithmetical accuracy of posting.
  • Types:
    • Balance method (most common)
    • Totals method
    • Totals-cum-balances
  • A TB that agrees is not conclusive proof of correct accounts. Errors of omission, principle, compensating errors and posting to the wrong account on the correct side all pass unnoticed.
  • Normal balances: assets, expenses, drawings, purchases, sales returns and opening stock are debit. Liabilities, capital, income, sales, purchase returns and provisions are credit.
  • Closing stock usually appears outside the TB and is given as an adjustment. It appears inside only when adjusted through purchases (then it is not shown again in the Trading A/c).

2. Classification of errors

ErrorMeaning / exampleTB affected?
Omission — completeTransaction not recorded at all (credit sale omitted from the sales book).No
Omission — partialRecorded in the book of original entry but one side not posted (e.g. not posted to the customer's account).Yes
Commission (clerical)
  • Wrong amount in the original book (₹4,500 recorded as ₹5,400 on both sides): TB not affected.
  • Wrong amount posted to one ledger account, wrong side, or casting / carry-forward / balancing errors: TB affected.
  • Posting to the wrong account of the same class on the correct side (Ram instead of Shyam): TB not affected.
Depends
PrincipleViolating capital/revenue distinction or accounting principle: furniture debited to Purchases, repairs capitalised, freight on new machine debited to freight outward, sale of old asset credited to Sales.No
CompensatingTwo errors cancel each other (Ram's account debited ₹100 short, Shyam's credited ₹100 short).No
One-sided errors (affect only one account) disturb the TB and go through the Suspense Account.
Two-sided errors (both accounts affected) do not disturb the TB and are rectified by a direct entry between the two accounts.

3. Suspense account

  • A temporary account opened for the TB difference so that final accounts can be prepared. If the debit total is short, the suspense account goes on the debit side.
  • When one-sided errors are found, rectifying entries go through suspense. When all errors are found, suspense closes to nil.
  • If a suspense balance remains at year-end, it is shown in the Balance Sheet: debit balance under other current assets, credit balance under other current liabilities.
  • Not every suspense correction changes profit. Correcting a debtor's or creditor's personal account changes only ledger balances.

4. Rectification method

Rule: compare (a) the entry that was made and (b) the entry that should have been made. Pass the difference.

ErrorRectifying entry
Furniture ₹50,000 bought on credit, debited to PurchasesFurniture Dr; To Purchases (profit was understated by 50,000; correction raises profit)
Repairs ₹8,000 debited to MachineryRepairs Dr; To Machinery (profit was overstated)
Sales book undercast ₹1,000Suspense Dr; To Sales
Credit sale ₹5,000 to Ram not posted to Ram's accountRam Dr; To Suspense
₹500 received from Mohan posted to the debit of his accountSuspense Dr; To Mohan ₹1,000 (twice the amount)
Credit sale ₹4,500 recorded in the sales book as ₹5,400Sales Dr; To Customer ₹900 (two-sided, no suspense)
Sold old machine ₹20,000 credited to SalesSales Dr; To Machinery

5. Worked case (exam pattern)

A TB disagrees and the difference goes to suspense. Errors found:

  1. Sales book overcast ₹10,000.
  2. Purchase of ₹7,500 from Ravi posted to his account as ₹5,700.
  3. Discount allowed ₹600 posted to the credit of Discount Received.
  4. Repairs ₹2,000 debited to Building.
  • TB effect:
    • (a) credit side excess 10,000
    • (b) credit side short 1,800
    • (c) debit side short 600 and credit side excess 600
    • (d) no effect
    Credit total exceeds debit by 10,000 − 1,800 + 1,200 = ₹9,400, so suspense opens on the debit side ₹9,400.
  • Profit effect of rectification:
    • (a) sales reduced → profit −10,000
    • (b) none (personal account)
    • (c) discount allowed +600 expense and discount received −600 income → profit −1,200
    • (d) repairs expensed → −2,000
    Net profit falls by ₹13,200.

6. Effect on financial statements (case questions)

  • Capital item debited to an expense (machine bought, entered in the purchases book):
    • Profit understated; fixed assets understated; TB agrees.
    • Depreciation for the period is also missing, which partly offsets the understatement.
    • Example: ₹18 lakh machine bought 1 Jan, 10% SLM → missing depreciation ₹45,000; profit understated by ₹17.55 lakh.
  • Credit sale completely omitted while stock records are correct: sales and debtors understated, so gross profit and receivables are understated. TB still agrees.
  • Expense capitalised: profit and assets overstated.
  • Rectification after books are closed (next year): nominal accounts are already closed, so use Profit & Loss Adjustment A/c instead of the nominal account (or a prior period item under AS 5). Real and personal accounts are rectified directly.

7. Adjusting and closing entries

  • Adjusting entries (accrual basis) at year-end: outstanding expenses, prepaid expenses, accrued income, income received in advance, depreciation, bad debts and provision, interest on capital/drawings, closing stock. They are required even if the TB agrees.
  • Closing entries transfer nominal accounts to the Trading and P&L A/c. Real and personal accounts are carried forward.
Traps:
  • Wrong amount in the book of original entry → both sides wrong → TB agrees. Wrong amount posted to one ledger account → TB disagrees.
  • Posting to the wrong side → double the amount to rectify.
  • Legal expenses for acquiring land debited to Land is correct, not an error of principle.
  • Error of principle never affects the TB but often affects profit and assets.
  • A suspense account is not opened for errors that don't affect the TB.
A5:
Syllabus: Cash book vs pass book, causes of difference, preparing a BRS, adjusting the cash book balance, advantages. Asked: 2 questions every session since June 2024. May 2026 asked:

  • which items need a cash-book entry vs which are timing differences
  • starting from an overdraft
  • CB ₹20,000 vs PB ₹28,000
  • a posting error vs an unpresented cheque

1. Mirror image

  • Your cash book (bank column) and the bank's pass book / statement record the same account from opposite sides.
  • A debit balance in the cash book = credit balance in the pass book = money in the bank (favourable).
  • An overdraft = credit balance in the cash book = debit balance in the pass book.
  • So the pass book is a mirror image only when there are no timing differences or errors, which is rare.

2. Causes of difference — sort them into three boxes

BoxItemsCash book entry needed?
A. Timing differences (in the CB, not yet in the bank)
  • Cheques issued but not yet presented
  • Cheques deposited but not yet collected/credited
No. They clear by themselves; show them only in the BRS.
B. Bank-originated items (in the bank, not yet in the CB)
  • Bank charges and commission
  • Interest credited or debited by the bank
  • Direct deposits by customers / NEFT received
  • Dividend or interest collected by the bank
  • Payments under standing instructions (insurance, EMI)
  • Dishonoured cheques
Yes. Update the cash book (adjusted cash book).
C. Errors
  • By the firm (wrong amount or side in the CB, casting errors): correct the CB.
  • By the bank (wrong debit or credit): show in the BRS and ask the bank to correct.
Firm's errors: Yes. Bank's errors: No.

3. Direction rules (starting from a favourable cash-book balance)

ItemStart: CB debit balance → find PB
Cheques issued, not presentedAdd (the bank hasn't reduced the balance yet)
Cheques deposited, not creditedLess
Interest / dividend / direct deposit credited by bankAdd
Bank charges, SI payment, interest on OD, dishonoured chequeLess

Shortcut: ask "is the bank's balance higher or lower than mine because of this item?"

  • Starting from the PB, reverse every sign.
  • Starting from an overdraft, treat it as a negative number and apply the same logic. Or use the rule: add what reduces the overdraft, subtract what increases it, and remember that items which raise a favourable balance reduce an overdraft.

4. Worked examples

(a) CB debit ₹40,000; cheques issued not presented ₹12,000; cheques deposited not cleared ₹8,000; bank charges ₹1,000 not in CB; interest credited ₹600.
PB = 40,000 + 12,000 − 8,000 − 1,000 + 600 = ₹43,600 (credit).

(b) CB overdraft ₹80,000; cheques issued not presented ₹15,000; cheques deposited not credited ₹22,000; bank charges ₹500; OD interest ₹2,500; direct deposit ₹12,000.
Treat as −80,000: −80,000 + 15,000 − 22,000 − 500 − 2,500 + 12,000 = −78,000 → overdraft ₹78,000 as per PB.

(c) Adjusted cash book first. CB ₹24.80 lakh. Dishonoured cheque ₹1.10 lakh, bank charges ₹12,500, dividend credited ₹95,000, SI insurance ₹48,000:
Adjusted CB = 24,80,000 − 1,10,000 − 12,500 + 95,000 − 48,000 = ₹23,04,500.
Then the BRS shows only the timing item: + unpresented cheques ₹4.20 lakh → PB ₹27,24,500.

(d) Error. A cheque deposited of ₹1,80,000 was entered in the CB as ₹18,000. The CB is understated by ₹1,62,000, so correct the cash book (it is not a timing difference).

5. Need and advantages

  • Detects errors and frauds.
  • Shows the true bank balance for the Balance Sheet (the adjusted cash-book balance goes to the Balance Sheet, not the pass-book balance).
  • Reveals stale or undelivered cheques and keeps a check on bank charges.
  • Prepared periodically (monthly). Banks reconcile their own nostro and inter-branch accounts similarly (chapter A9).
Traps:
  • "All items only in the BRS, no CB entry": wrong. Bank-originated items need CB entries.
  • An unpresented cheque is the only classic item that never needs a CB entry.
  • In the Balance Sheet, show the adjusted CB balance.
  • Overdraft questions reverse your instinct: an unpresented cheque reduces the overdraft per pass book.
  • A cheque recorded in the CB but deposited late = timing (deposited, not credited).
A6:
Syllabus: Meaning, causes, need and factors of depreciation; entries; SLM, WDV, units of production, sum-of-years'-digits; replacement and sinking fund; amortisation. Asked: 4–5 questions every session from May 2025 onwards (it was 1–2 earlier). May 2026 asked:

  • SLM carrying amount
  • WDV book value after 3 years
  • choosing a method to match the benefit pattern
  • revision of life or residual value
  • zero carrying amount under SLM
  • sinking fund

1. Basics

  • Depreciation = allocation of the depreciable amount (cost − residual value) over the useful life. It is allocation of cost, not valuation.
  • It is a non-cash expense: it reduces profit but no cash goes out. That is why it is added back in the cash flow statement.
  • Causes: wear and tear, efflux of time (leases, patents), obsolescence (technology), depletion (mines).
  • Factors: cost, residual (salvage) value, useful life, method.
  • Starts when the asset is available for use, even if not yet used.
  • Land is not depreciated (unlimited life), except quarries and mines, which are depleted.
  • Companies Act Schedule II gives useful lives. Residual value is normally not more than 5% of original cost; a higher figure must be justified. Each significant component is depreciated separately (component approach, AS 10).
  • Depreciation is also called amortisation for intangibles and depletion for wasting assets.

2. Methods

MethodFormulaPattern / suits
Straight line (SLM)(Cost − Residual) ÷ Useful lifeEqual charge each year. Suits assets giving even benefit (buildings, furniture, leases). Book value can reach zero (or the residual value).
Written down value (WDV)Fixed % on the opening book value. Rate r = 1 − (S/C)1/nHigher charge early, lower later. Suits assets whose benefit is front-loaded and whose repairs rise later (plant, vehicles). Book value never reaches zero. The Income-tax Act uses WDV on blocks of assets.
Units of production(Cost − Residual) × Units this year ÷ Total estimated unitsCharge varies with use (machines, mines).
Sum of years' digits (SYD)(Cost − Residual) × Remaining life at start of the year ÷ [n(n+1)/2]Accelerated: declining charge.
Sinking fundEqual annual amount is set aside and invested, so that with interest it accumulates to the replacement cost.Provides cash for replacement (also used for debenture redemption).

Combined effect: under SLM, depreciation is constant and repairs rise, so the total burden rises. Under WDV, depreciation falls as repairs rise, so the total is more even. That is the classic argument for WDV.

3. Worked numbers (practise until automatic)

  1. SLM with installation and residual: machine ₹48 lakh + installation ₹2 lakh, residual ₹5 lakh, life 9 years.
    • Annual depreciation = (50 − 5) ÷ 9 = ₹5 lakh.
    • After 3 years: 50 − 15 = ₹35 lakh.
  2. WDV: ₹3,00,000 at 20% for 3 years → 3,00,000 × 0.8³ = ₹1,53,600. ₹4,00,000 at 20%, end of year 2 = ₹2,56,000.
  3. Part year, SLM: ₹5,00,000 bought 1 Oct 2020, life 5 years, nil salvage. Depreciation is ₹1,00,000 a year. To 31 Mar 2024 that is 3.5 years = ₹3,50,000.
  4. Part year, WDV: ₹2,40,000 bought 1 Jul 2024 at 15%.
    • FY 24-25: 2,40,000 × 15% × 9/12 = 27,000.
    • FY 25-26: (2,40,000 − 27,000) × 15% = 31,950.
  5. Units: cost ₹12 lakh, residual ₹2 lakh, total capacity 1,00,000 units, year-1 output 18,000 units → 10,00,000 × 18% = ₹1,80,000.
  6. SYD: cost ₹6,50,000, salvage ₹50,000, life 5 years. Sum of digits = 15.
    • Year 1 = 5/15 × 6,00,000 = 2,00,000.
    • Year 2 = 4/15 × 6,00,000 = 1,60,000.
  7. Sale of asset: ₹5,00,000 bought 1 Apr 2023, WDV 20%, sold 30 Sep 2025 for ₹2,80,000.
    • Book value: 4,00,000 (end FY 23-24) → 3,20,000 (end FY 24-25) → less half-year 32,000 = 2,88,000.
    • Loss ₹8,000, charged to P&L.
  8. Revision of estimate (AS 10 / AS 5): cost ₹1.80 crore, life 10 years, residual ₹20 lakh, so depreciation is ₹16 lakh a year.
    • After 5 years the carrying amount is ₹1 crore.
    • The residual value is revised to ₹8 lakh with the same remaining life of 5 years.
    • New charge = (100 − 8) ÷ 5 = ₹18.4 lakh a year. Past years are not restated.

4. Accounting entries

  • Without provision: Depreciation Dr; To Asset A/c. The asset is shown at WDV.
  • With provision for depreciation (accumulated depreciation): Depreciation Dr; To Provision for Depreciation. The asset stays at cost, and the provision is deducted in the Balance Sheet.
  • On sale with a provision: transfer cost to an Asset Disposal A/c, transfer the accumulated depreciation, credit the sale proceeds; the balance is profit or loss.
  • Sinking fund:
    • Each year: Depreciation Dr; To Sinking Fund. Then Sinking Fund Investment Dr; To Bank.
    • Interest received: Bank Dr; To Sinking Fund (reinvested).
    • The fund only provides money. It does not remove the obligation to repay or replace.

5. Changes

  • Under AS 10, the method, useful life and residual value are reviewed at least at each financial year-end.
  • Any change is a change in accounting estimate and is applied prospectively: the remaining carrying amount less the new residual value is spread over the remaining life.
  • No restatement of past years.
  • Revaluation: depreciation is then charged on the revalued amount. An increase goes to revaluation surplus; a decrease goes to P&L (unless it reverses an earlier surplus).
Traps:
  • Installation, freight and trial-run costs are added to cost before computing depreciation.
  • WDV can never bring an asset to exactly zero. SLM with nil residual can.
  • "Higher early benefits, rising maintenance later" → WDV. "Benefits even over time" → SLM. "Benefits depend on output" → units of production.
  • Depreciation is not a source of funds. It only avoids an outflow of profit as dividend (retains funds).
  • A change of method is now a change in estimate (AS 10), not a change in policy.
  • Depreciation on an asset bought mid-year: SLM and WDV are both time-proportionate unless told "full year's depreciation in the year of purchase".
A7:
Syllabus: Capital vs revenue expenditure, receipts. In the May 2026 paper it came with AS 10. Asked: 1–2 questions every session, plus 2–3 hidden inside golden-rule and error questions. May 2026 asked:

  • Is every machinery cost debited to Machinery?
  • Major inspection cost (AS 10)
  • Kiln: freight, installation, maintenance, major part replacement
  • ₹5,000 replacement of a worn-out part

1. The test

Capital expenditureRevenue expenditure
BenefitLasts more than one yearUsed up within the year
PurposeAcquire, extend, improve or enhance a fixed asset (capacity, life, efficiency, cost reduction)Maintain the asset in its existing condition; day-to-day running
Shown inBalance Sheet (asset), then depreciatedP&L of the year
RecurrenceNon-recurring generallyRecurring

2. AS 10 — what goes into the cost of PPE

Capitalise (include in cost)Do NOT capitalise (expense)
  • Purchase price, import duties, non-refundable taxes, less trade discounts and rebates
  • Site preparation
  • Initial delivery and handling (freight inward)
  • Installation and assembly, including wages of own staff for installation
  • Testing, less net proceeds of samples produced during testing
  • Professional fees (architects, engineers)
  • Initial estimate of dismantling and site-restoration cost
  • Borrowing cost on a qualifying asset (AS 16)
  • Costs of opening a new facility
  • Introducing a new product (advertising, promotion)
  • Doing business in a new location or with a new class of customers (staff training)
  • Administration and general overheads
  • Costs after the asset is ready (initial operating losses, idle time)
  • Relocation or reorganisation
  • Refundable GST / input tax credit available

3. Subsequent costs (after the asset is in use)

  • Day-to-day servicing (labour, consumables, small parts, lubricants, AMC): expense.
  • Replacement of a significant part (kiln lining, aircraft seats, engine): capitalise if the recognition criteria are met, and derecognise the carrying amount of the replaced part (component approach).
  • Major inspection (e.g. a statutory overhaul every 5 years, without which the asset cannot operate): capitalise as a component if the recognition criteria are met, even though no new part is fitted. Derecognise any remaining cost of the previous inspection.
  • Repairs to a second-hand asset to make it usable at purchase: capital. Later regular repairs: revenue.
  • Spare parts and stand-by equipment used for more than one period: PPE. Others are inventory.

4. Classic examples

ItemNature
Freight and cartage on a new machineCapital
Freight on goods purchasedRevenue (part of cost of goods, Trading A/c)
Legal fees for buying land; registration and stamp dutyCapital
White-washing / painting an existing building annuallyRevenue
Addition of a new floor; extension of buildingCapital
Replacing a worn-out small part to keep the machine runningRevenue
Overhaul raising capacity or extending lifeCapital
Interest on loan for construction until readyCapital (AS 16); after that, revenue
Preliminary expenses (company formation)Now expensed when incurred (AS 26). Can be written off against Securities Premium (Sec 52).
Heavy advertising for a new productTraditionally "deferred revenue expenditure". Now expensed (AS 26 does not allow carry-forward).
Development of software / patent registrationCapital if AS 26 criteria are met

5. Receipts

  • Capital receipts:
    • issue of shares or debentures
    • loans raised
    • sale proceeds of fixed assets
    • insurance claim for loss of a fixed asset
    • capital subsidy
  • Revenue receipts:
    • sales
    • interest, dividend, rent and commission received
    • insurance claim for loss of stock
    • discount received
    • bad debts recovered
  • Profit on sale of a fixed asset is a capital profit. In practice it is shown in P&L as other income, but it is not sales.

6. Why the distinction matters

  • If capital expenditure is treated as revenue: profit understated, assets understated (secret reserve).
  • If revenue expenditure is capitalised: profit and assets overstated (window dressing).
  • Either way it is an error of principle, and the Trial Balance still agrees (chapter A4).
Traps:
  • "It relates to machinery, so debit Machinery": wrong if it is routine maintenance or lubricants.
  • Major statutory inspection with no new part → can still be capitalised (AS 10).
  • Installation wages paid to own employees → capital, not Wages A/c.
  • Refundable GST is not part of cost; non-refundable duties are.
  • Training staff on a new machine → revenue.
A8:
Syllabus: Instruments of credit, term and due date, important terms, accounting entries, accommodation bill, bill books. Asked: 2–5 questions every session (terms plus entries). Favourites:

  • Due-date calculation with days of grace and a holiday
  • Accommodation bill
  • Entries for discounting, endorsement, collection and dishonour
  • Rebate on retiring a bill
  • Bill vs promissory note statements

1. Instruments (Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881)

Bill of exchange (Sec 5)Promissory note (Sec 4)Cheque (Sec 6)
NatureUnconditional orderUnconditional promiseBill drawn on a specified banker, payable on demand (includes electronic cheques and truncated cheque images)
Parties3: drawer, drawee (acceptor), payee (drawer and payee may be the same)2: maker, payee3: drawer, bank (drawee), payee
AcceptanceNeeded (for time bills)Not neededNot needed
Days of grace3 days for time bills3 days (if payable after time)None (always on demand)
Noting / protestPossible on dishonourPossibleNot needed
Payable to bearer on demand?Not allowedCannot be made payable to bearer (only RBI/Govt may issue such notes, Sec 31 RBI Act)Allowed

2. Key terms

  • Drawer: the creditor who draws the bill. Drawee: the debtor on whom it is drawn; after accepting, the acceptor.
  • Payee: the person to be paid.
  • Holder: entitled in his own name to possession and to receive payment.
  • Holder in due course: took it for consideration, before maturity, in good faith.
  • Tenor / usance: the period of the bill.
  • Sight / demand bill: payable on presentation, no grace days.
  • After-date bill: period counted from the date of drawing. After-sight bill: counted from the date of acceptance.
  • Endorsement: signing on the back to transfer. Endorser → endorsee.
  • Discounting: selling the bill to a bank before maturity for less than face value.
  • Dishonour: by non-acceptance or non-payment.
  • Noting: a notary public records the fact of dishonour. Noting charges are paid by the holder and recovered from the drawee.
  • Protest: a formal certificate of dishonour by a notary.
  • Retiring a bill: the acceptor pays before the due date and the holder allows a rebate, i.e. a discount for the unexpired period.
  • Renewal: the old bill is cancelled and a new bill is drawn, usually with interest, when the acceptor can't pay.
  • Trade bill: backed by a genuine sale of goods.
  • Accommodation bill: drawn and accepted without consideration, only to raise funds by discounting. It is legally enforceable by a holder in due course, but there is no underlying trade, so credit risk is higher. Banks are told to avoid discounting accommodation bills. Sec 43: the accommodating party is not liable to the party accommodated.

3. Due date (maturity)

  • Due date = date of drawing (or acceptance, for after-sight bills) + tenor + 3 days of grace.
  • Months: calendar months. If the due month has no corresponding date, use its last day.
  • Days: exclude the day of drawing.
  • If the due date is a public holiday, the bill is due on the preceding business day (Sec 25).
BillWorkingDue date
Drawn 13 May 2023, 1 month13 Jun + 316 June 2023
Drawn 23 Nov 2024, 2 months23 Jan + 3 = 26 Jan 2025, Republic Day → preceding day25 January 2025
Drawn 31 Jan 2026, 1 monthFeb has no 31st → 28 Feb + 33 March 2026
Drawn 10 Jan 2026, 90 days after dateJan 21 days + Feb 28 + Mar 31 = 80 → 10 more days = 10 Apr; + 313 April 2026
Accepted 5 Mar 2026, 2 months after sight5 May + 38 May 2026

4. Entries (drawer's books = holder)

EventDrawer / holderDrawee / acceptor
Bill drawn and acceptedBills Receivable Dr; To DebtorCreditor Dr; To Bills Payable
(a) Held till maturity, paidCash Dr; To B/RB/P Dr; To Cash
(b) Discounted with bankBank Dr + Discount Dr; To B/RNo entry
(c) Endorsed to a creditorCreditor Dr; To B/RNo entry
(d) Sent to bank for collectionBills sent for collection Dr; To B/R. On collection: Bank Dr; To BSFCNo entry
Dishonour (bill with holder)Debtor Dr; To B/R (+ noting charges: Debtor Dr; To Cash)B/P Dr + Noting charges Dr; To Creditor
Dishonour (bill discounted)Debtor Dr; To Bank (bank recovers from drawer)same as above
Dishonour (bill endorsed)Debtor Dr; To Creditor (endorsee)same as above
Retired earlyCash Dr + Rebate on bills Dr; To B/RB/P Dr; To Cash + Rebate on bills (income)
  • Discount on a discounted bill = face value × rate × unexpired period. It is a finance cost for the drawer. Sales were already recorded when the goods were sold.
  • Bill books: the Bills Receivable Book and Bills Payable Book (subsidiary books).
Traps:
  • No days of grace for demand/sight bills and cheques.
  • "Legal acceptance makes it a genuine trade bill": wrong. Acceptance makes it enforceable, not genuine.
  • An after-sight bill counts from acceptance.
  • When a discounted bill is dishonoured, the drawer credits Bank, not B/R.
  • Rebate on retiring a bill is an expense for the holder and income for the acceptor.
A9:
Syllabus: Bank audit, emergence of risk-based internal audit, types of bank audit (concurrent, internal, statutory), role of audit and inspection; back-office functions; reconciliation of inter-branch / office entries; peculiar features of bank accounting. Asked: 2–3 audit questions plus about 1 back-office question per session. May 2026 asked:

  • A forensic audit approach
  • RBI audit reports
  • Inter-branch reconciliation
  • Functions to ensure compliance

1. Types of bank audit

AuditBy whomPurpose / features
Statutory audit (central + branch)External CA firms; appointment needs RBI approval (Sec 30, BR Act). For PSBs the bank appoints from RBI's approved list.True-and-fair opinion on annual accounts. Also gives the Long Form Audit Report (LFAR) to management and RBI on advances, deposits, internal controls and NPAs.
  • RBI 2021 guidelines: SCA/SA term of 3 continuous years, then a 6-year cooling-off.
Concurrent auditExternal CAs or the bank's own (retired/serving) officersExamines transactions at the same time or soon after they occur. It is a part of the internal audit system, an early-warning tool.
  • Covers treasury, large branches and high-risk areas.
  • Reports go to the controlling office / Audit Committee.
Internal audit / inspectionThe bank's Inspection & Audit DepartmentPeriodic review of compliance, controls and risk management.
  • Since 2002, banks have moved to Risk-Based Internal Audit (RBIA): audit frequency and depth depend on each branch's risk rating.
  • RBI made RBIA compulsory for large NBFCs and UCBs in 2021.
RBI inspection / supervisionRBI under Sec 35, BR ActEarlier CAMELS-based Annual Financial Inspection. Now Risk-Based Supervision (RBS, from 2013; SPARC model). Covers capital, asset quality, management, earnings, liquidity and systems. Includes the Risk Assessment Report.
Revenue / income auditInternal or externalChecks leakage of income: interest, charges, commission.
Credit / stock auditExternal auditors appointed by the bankPhysical verification of a borrower's stock and receivables, drawing power, end use (for large working-capital limits).
IS / IT auditSpecialistsSecurity and integrity of CBS and data, access controls.
Forensic auditForensic specialistsInvestigates suspected fraud with evidence that can stand in court:
  • trace funds (end-use)
  • verify the existence of suppliers and buyers
  • examine digital evidence
  • rebuild the transaction trail
  • then fix responsibility
Ratio comparisons or reworking drawing power cannot prove a coordinated fraud.

Audit Committee of the Board (ACB) oversees the audit function and follows up on inspection and LFAR findings. Audit vs inspection: audit checks that the books are accurate and fair; inspection is wider (management, compliance, risk, systems).

2. Peculiar features of bank accounting

  • Transactions are recorded first in the customer's (personal) ledger through vouchers on the same day. The day book and general ledger are built from them. Every transaction is supported by a voucher.
  • Voucher system:
    • debit and credit vouchers
    • composite / transfer voucher (a single voucher with several debits and credits, used when one debit/credit affects many accounts)
    • clearing vouchers
    • Vouchers are verified and authorised by an officer other than the maker (maker–checker).
  • Slip system / cash book slip system:
    • Pay-in slips filled by customers act as vouchers.
    • The cash book is maintained through slips sorted by type.
    • This saves posting time.
  • Daily balancing: general ledger and subsidiary ledgers are balanced every day. CBS does this automatically, end of day.
  • Accrual for interest and income recognition norms for NPAs (no accrual of interest on NPAs).

3. Back-office functions

  • The back office supports the front office (customer-facing). Its work:
    • transaction processing and settlement (clearing, NEFT/RTGS)
    • reconciliation
    • account maintenance and KYC data
    • MIS and regulatory returns
    • loan documentation and limit monitoring
    • compliance checks
  • In treasury: front office (dealing), mid office (risk management, limits), back office (deal confirmation, settlement, accounting, reconciliation). These are kept separate for internal control.

4. Reconciliation in banks

  • Inter-branch / inter-office accounts:
    • Branches transact with each other on behalf of customers through Inter-Branch (IB) / Head Office accounts.
    • The originating branch sends an advice and the responding branch records the matching entry.
    • Entries without a matching response are unreconciled.
  • Why it matters: long-pending unreconciled debits can hide frauds or losses.
  • RBI's rule on inter-branch accounts:
    • banks must eliminate old outstanding entries
    • banks must provide 100% for net debit balances outstanding for more than one year
    • credit balances are not taken to income
  • Also reconciled:
    • Nostro accounts: our account with a foreign bank, in foreign currency. Matched with our mirror account.
    • Vostro accounts
    • ATM and card settlement, clearing differences
    • suspense and sundry accounts
  • With CBS, centralised reconciliation cells match entries using automated tools.
Traps:
  • Concurrent audit is a part of internal audit. It is not a statutory audit.
  • LFAR is given by statutory auditors.
  • RBI inspection is under Sec 35; auditors and their RBI approval under Sec 30; accounts and Third Schedule format under Sec 29 (all BR Act).
  • Unreconciled inter-branch debits are the risk. The 100% provision is on net debit balances older than 1 year.
  • Forensic audit = tracing evidence and money trail, not profitability review.
